name: Turkmen
variety: Standard Turkmen (based on the Teke dialect), Latin script
sources: Clark, Larry (1998). Turkmen Reference Grammar. Harrassowitz.
Hoey, Elliott Michael (2013). Grammatical Sketch of Turkmen. MA thesis, University of California, Santa Barbara.
Schönig, Claus (1998). Turkmen. In Lars Johanson & Éva Á. Csató (eds.), The Turkic Languages. Routledge.
contrasts: phonemic vowel length, inherited from Proto-Turkic and not written: at [ɑt] 'horse' versus at [ɑːt] 'name', ot [ot] 'grass' versus ot [oːt] 'fire'
dental fricatives /θ ð/ (spelt s, z) where other Turkic languages have /s z/
front versus back and rounded versus unrounded vowels
voiced versus voiceless stops and affricates
short /e/ pairs with long /æː/ (spelt ä); long /eː/ and short /æ/ are marginal
allophony: /θ ð/ are interdental or dental fricatives in all positions
/b/ is a stop word-initially and a bilabial fricative or approximant [β] after vowels; the letter w is also [β ~ w]
/ɡ/ is a stop word-initially and a fricative [ɣ] (front words) or [ʁ] (back words) between vowels and finally
/k/ is uvular [q] and /h/ is [x ~ χ] next to back vowels
/l/ is velarised next to back vowels
rounding harmony goes further in speech than in spelling: written a and e after a rounded vowel are pronounced [o] and [ø] (dogan [doʁon]), written y and i as [u] and [y]
progressive assimilation in clusters, not written: ld > ll, nd > nn, zd > ðð, sd > θθ
/f/ occurs in loans and is often bilabial [ɸ]
phonotactics: no onset clusters in native words
coda clusters are sonorant + obstruent (dört, gurt)
backness harmony throughout the word; rounding harmony is written only in part (high vowels of the second syllable), and the rounding of low vowels is never written
long vowels occur in any syllable; suffixes can create long vowels by contraction

stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word; some suffixes and particles (negation, question and predicative endings) are unstressed and leave the stress on the preceding syllable.
stress.cues: not instrumentally studied in the sources used; vowel length is independent of stress

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; short high vowels are very short and may be dropped between voiceless consonants
rhythm.notes: No instrumental rhythm study is known to me; because vowel length is phonemic, syllable durations vary more than in Turkish.

length.notes: Every short vowel except /e/ has a long counterpart. The spelling does not show length, apart from ä (nearly always long) and üý. Geminates arise from assimilation (ll, nn, θθ, ðð) and in numerals. No published duration ratio is given here.

intonation.declarative: falling at the end of the statement
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the clause-final particle -my/-mi; the pitch pattern is not documented in the sources used
intonation.wh_question: question word in preverbal position; pitch pattern not documented in the sources used
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: rise to a high on the final stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Low confidence: no instrumental study of Turkmen intonation was available to me; the entries follow the general pattern of the better described Turkic languages (Turkish, Kazakh).

problems: no stress rule is set for tk, so the default penultimate stress applies (kitap, sagat, dogan are stressed on the first syllable); Turkmen stress is final, and only a few suffix rules mark it

vowel length is not written, and eSpeak gets it only from a list of about 870 respelt word forms (tk_listx): forms not listed lose the long vowel (kitap has [ɑː], kitaplar does not) and homographs such as at 'horse' and at 'name' cannot be told apart
word-initial b is turned into [β] after any preceding word and into [m] after a word ending in a nasal, whatever the phrasing (sen biz gives [θen mið])
the ipa string of the long vowel ɯː has no length mark (affects --ipa output only)
good: s and z are the dental fricatives [θ ð]
the vowels ɯ (y), ø (ö), y (ü) and æ (ä) are all present, short and long
unwritten rounding harmony is applied by rule (dogan gives [doʁon])
k, g and h get uvular or fricative allophones by vowel context, and ld, nd, sd, zd assimilate
long vowels exist as phonemes with twice the length of short ones (300 versus 150)

notes: Short /æ/ and long /eː/ occur in a handful of words only and are left out of the vowel list. The degree of aspiration of the voiceless stops is not documented in the sources used; eSpeak NG uses the unaspirated base2 stops.
